tool.name: kev_diff_check
tool.description:
Force a CISA KEV catalog refresh, diff against the prior cached snapshot, and emit info findings for new entries since the last scan. Second 🟡 important item from the §10 expert-pentester gap audit. Extends #9 (which lazy-loads KEV with a 24h cache) into a daily-scan workflow — each run highlights newly-actively-exploited CVEs the customer should drop other priorities to patch.
Mechanism: 1. Forces KEV refresh via `strix.telemetry.threat_intel.KevCatalog.refresh(force=True)` (the existing #9 cache). 2. Reads prior snapshot from `~/.strix/kev_diff_snapshot.json` (override via `STRIX_KEV_DIFF_SNAPSHOT` env var; small file storing just the sorted CVE-ID list + timestamp). 3. Computes set diff: - **Added**: CVEs in current catalog but not in snapshot. Each emits an info finding with full KEV metadata (vendor / product / vuln_name / added_at / due_date / required_action / ransomware_use). - **Removed**: CVEs in snapshot but not in current catalog. Recorded in the result for the agent (CISA occasionally retires KEV entries) but no finding emitted. 4. Updates the snapshot to the current catalog.
First-run behaviour: silently baselines the snapshot, emits zero findings (no flooding on first use). Use `include_first_run_findings=True` to override (capped at 50 findings) for one-shot scans where the operator wants a baseline KEV report.
Findings tagged `category=vulnerable_software`, `cwe=CWE-1395`, with the CVE attached so the tracer's existing KEV enrichment auto-decorates with the full record. Severity=info (the tool is informational about the catalog itself; downstream `cve_lookup` (#61) / `nvd_lookup` (#73) surface the actual exploitability per CVE). `verification_status=verified` since CISA KEV is authoritative.
Hard cap of 50 findings per run to prevent flooding when first-run findings are enabled.
MITRE techniques: T1592.002 (Software fingerprint) + T1588.006 (Obtain Vulnerabilities).
Composes with cluster-A safety. The KEV fetch goes through `strix.telemetry.threat_intel._fetch_json` (stdlib urllib), not the proxy chain — `--exclude-path` doesn't apply (URL is CISA's, not the customer's).

parameter.name: timeout
parameter.description: Underlying HTTP timeout (advisory — KEV fetcher uses stdlib urllib with its own timeout). Default 30.

parameter.name: force_refresh
parameter.description: When True (default), forces a fresh KEV download regardless of the existing 24h cache. Set False to defer to whatever the cache has (useful for repeated calls within a single scan).

parameter.name: include_first_run_findings
parameter.description: When True, the first run (no prior snapshot) emits findings for ALL existing KEV entries (capped at 50). Default False — first run silently establishes the baseline so daily-scan workflows aren't flooded on day one.

returns.description:
{success, total_kev_entries, snapshotted_cve_count, prior_snapshot_at, snapshot_updated, first_run, new_entries: [{cve_id, vendor, product, vuln_name, added_at, due_date, required_action, ransomware_use}, ...], removed_entries: [cve_id, ...], findings_emitted, error?}.
The agent should: 1. Treat findings emitted by this tool as **highest-priority context** — they represent CVEs CISA has confirmed are being actively exploited, with binding patch deadlines for federal agencies. 2. For each new entry, cross-reference with `cve_lookup` (#61) / `nvd_lookup` (#73) to confirm whether the customer's detected stack is affected. 3. For ransomware-flagged entries (`ransomware_use=Known`), escalate above other newly-emerged CVEs.
